overview: Democrats won control of Congress in Tuesday's midterm elections, and Vice President JD Vance said the Iran war was the reason Republicans lost. House Speaker Mike Johnson's future and Hakeem Jeffries' path to the speakership are drawing attention. Wall Street rallied after the results, with the Dow up about 3%, while oil stayed near $100 a barrel. Abroad, bomb threats diverted flights across Europe and a hack drew attention to French blood-bank systems.

stories.headline: Democrats projected to win both the House and the Senate in the midterms
stories.summary: NBC News and CBS News projected that Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress in Tuesday's midterm elections. Democrats flipped a large number of Republican-held House seats and several Senate seats, including some in Republican-leaning states. Democratic leaders said they would use the majorities to check President Trump, and outlets described the result as setting up two years of possible deadlock.
stories.why_it_matters: Divided government means the president's agenda needs Democratic votes in Congress, and Democratic-run committees can now investigate the administration. Spending bills, nominations and oversight of the Iran war are all likely to become more contested.
stories.background: Before the election Republicans held the House by a narrow margin and the Senate 53-47, and Democrats needed a net gain of three House seats and four Senate seats for control. The midterms were widely framed as a verdict on President Trump, whose approval rating was low and whose war with Iran, launched with Israel, has run for about nine months. Gas prices and the cost of living were also major issues. Control of the chambers decides which party sets the legislative agenda and chairs committees from January.

facts.text: NBC News projected that Democrats won control of both the House and the Senate.
CBS News separately projected a Democratic House majority and a Democratic Senate majority, with several upset wins in red states.
CBS News reported Democrats flipped more than two dozen Republican-held House seats.
Fox News reported Democrats scored seven Senate and 27 House pickups.
The Hindu reported it will be the first time Trump has faced Democratic control of both chambers during a term in the White House.
Democrats vowed to use the win to rein in Trump, setting up possible deadlock in Washington, according to a wire report carried by Daily Maverick.
Before the election Republicans held the House 218-214 and the Senate 53-47.

stories.headline: Vance blames the Iran war for Republican midterm losses; Trump says he would do it again
stories.summary: Vice President JD Vance wrote a roughly 600-word post on X saying the Iran war was the reason Republicans lost, in one of his sharpest breaks with President Trump. The New York Times reported he did so with Trump's apparent approval. Trump acknowledged the war affected the vote, pointing to high gas prices, but said he would have gone ahead with it anyway.
stories.why_it_matters: The war's unpopularity is now a open argument inside the Republican Party, and what Trump does next on Iran will affect gas prices, troop deployments and the Democratic Congress's response.
stories.background: The United States and Israel launched a war against Iran roughly nine months ago, and it has continued with efforts to end it so far unsuccessful. Polling before the election showed it was unpopular, including among some Trump supporters. Vance had earlier defended the effort and in a pre-election interview said he would not call it a war. He is widely seen as a possible 2028 presidential candidate.

facts.text: Vance wrote in a post on X that "the reason we lost is the war," per Axios.
The New York Times reported that Vance's critique came with Trump's apparent approval.
Trump acknowledged the war affected the midterms, suggesting voters were frustrated by surging gas prices.
Trump said he would do it again, and CBS reported he said he would have launched the war anyway.
Iran said the U.S. election results show Americans reject the war, per CBS News.
Before the election, Vance told reporters he would not call the Iran fight a war.

stories.headline: Mississippi Senate race too close to call, with no recount procedure
stories.summary: Democrat Scott Colom was ahead of Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith by dozens of votes in the BBC's overnight report, and the race remained unresolved Wednesday as thousands of provisional ballots were counted. The Hill reported Mississippi has no recount procedure, so the result could end up in court. A Colom win would make him the first Black U.S. senator elected in the state since 1875.
stories.why_it_matters: The outcome could decide the size of the new Senate Democratic majority and shows how far the Republican losses reached into deep-red states. A court fight would delay a final result.
stories.background: Hyde-Smith is the Republican incumbent in a state Trump won by about 23 points in 2024, per pre-election reporting. Colom is a district attorney who won the Democratic nomination in March. Polls before the election showed Hyde-Smith ahead, and an independent, Ty Pinkins, was also on the ballot. Alaska's Senate race was also reported as tight.

facts.text: The BBC reported Colom led by dozens of votes.
Thousands of provisional ballots were still being counted, the BBC reported.
CBS News described the race as a toss-up with a razor-thin margin on Wednesday morning.
The Hill reported that Mississippi has no recount procedure and the contest could end up in the courts.
A Colom victory would make him the first Black U.S. senator elected in Mississippi since 1875, per the BBC.
Pre-election polling had Hyde-Smith ahead by about 6 points, with independent Ty Pinkins at 7 percent.

stories.headline: Jeffries launches speaker bid as Johnson steps aside and Scalise and Jordan vie to lead House Republicans
stories.summary: House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries formally launched his bid for speaker in a letter to colleagues, and Politico reported he is expected to face no competition. He would be the first Black speaker. Speaker Mike Johnson told Republicans he will not run for minority leader, and Majority Leader Steve Scalise and Rep. Jim Jordan announced bids for the job.
stories.why_it_matters: The people who lead the House set which bills get votes and which investigations start, so these choices shape what Congress does on spending, oversight and the Iran war.
stories.background: Republicans held the House majority with Johnson as speaker until Tuesday's election, when Democrats won a majority. Jeffries, of New York, has led the House Democrats as minority leader. Leadership elections inside each party's caucus take place before the new Congress convenes in January, and the full House then votes for speaker.

facts.text: Jeffries launched his bid for speaker in a letter to colleagues, per Axios.
Politico reported he is likely to cruise to the speakership with no expected competition.
AP reported he is poised to be the first Black speaker of the House.
Johnson told staffers he will not run for minority leader in the new Congress, per CBS News, a source familiar said.
Scalise and Jordan are both seeking to lead House Republicans.

stories.headline: Voters back abortion rights and voter ID in state ballot measures
stories.summary: Voters in dozens of states decided nearly 150 statewide ballot measures on Tuesday. Abortion-rights measures passed or were protected in several states including Missouri, Nevada and Virginia, and voter ID measures also passed. ABC News reported voters rejected Trump-backed redistricting measures.
stories.why_it_matters: Ballot measures change state law directly, affecting abortion access, voting rules and congressional district maps in the affected states.
stories.background: Many states let voters amend their constitutions or pass laws directly. Abortion has been on the ballot in many states since the Supreme Court ended the federal right in 2022. Redistricting fights over congressional maps have grown since President Trump urged states to redraw districts before the midterms.

facts.text: ABC News reported abortion-rights advocates won in Missouri, Nevada and Virginia.
The Guardian reported voters in Nevada, Virginia, Missouri and Idaho passed or strengthened reproductive rights protections.
NBC News said nearly 150 ballot measures were at stake in more than three dozen states, and NPR counted 146 statewide measures.

stories.headline: Abdul El-Sayed wins Michigan Senate race over Mike Rogers
stories.summary: Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, a progressive backed by Bernie Sanders and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, won Michigan's open Senate seat over Republican Mike Rogers, according to multiple outlets. Coverage came from both sides, with right-leaning outlets covering it more heavily. Many reports focused on what the win means for the Democratic Party.
stories.why_it_matters: The win adds a progressive to a new Democratic Senate majority and signals which wing of the party gained from the midterms, which could shape Democratic priorities.
stories.background: El-Sayed, a physician and former Detroit health director, won the Democratic nomination in a contested primary. Rep. Haley Stevens, who lost that primary, endorsed Rogers, the Republican nominee, days before the election. New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani praised the win.

stories.headline: Hong Kong court sentences activist Joshua Wong to 10 more years under the national security law
stories.summary: A Hong Kong court sentenced pro-democracy activist Joshua Wong, 30, to 10 years in prison in his second national security case, after he pleaded guilty to conspiracy to collude with foreign forces. The Financial Times reports the sentence pushes his expected release date to 2036. Wong has been in custody since 2020.
stories.why_it_matters: The case shows how far Hong Kong's legal environment has changed since 2020, which matters to anyone with business, family or travel ties to the city. It is also a marker for how foreign governments and rights groups may respond to Beijing's security law.
stories.background: Joshua Wong rose to prominence as a teenager during the 2014 Umbrella Movement protests for democratic elections in Hong Kong. Beijing imposed a national security law on the city in 2020, after which most of the pro-democracy movement's leaders were jailed or left. Wong has been in prison since 2020 and is the only activist in Hong Kong prosecuted twice under the law, according to The Guardian. Critics say the law has been used to dismantle the opposition, while Hong Kong and Beijing authorities say it restored stability.

facts.text: Joshua Wong was sentenced to 10 years in prison in a second case brought under the Beijing-imposed national security law.
The New York Times reports he was accused of conspiracy to collude with foreign forces; The Guardian says he earlier pleaded guilty.
Wong is 30 and has been in prison since 2020; the Financial Times says the sentence moves his expected release to 2036.
The BBC says Wong is among hundreds of Hongkongers detained under the law.

stories.headline: Wave of bomb threats diverts and disrupts flights across Europe
stories.summary: Bomb threats against passenger flights across Europe on Thursday led several planes to divert or land under military escort. The first reported case was an Aer Lingus flight from Dublin to Rome that landed at a French air base in Evreux with 151 passengers and six crew, the French prime minister's office said. Outlets report between seven and about 15 flights affected so far.
stories.why_it_matters: Travellers in Europe may face delays, diversions and extra security checks while the threats continue. Officials and experts have not said who is behind them.
stories.background: Bomb threats against aircraft are usually hoaxes but are treated seriously, which can mean diversions, military escorts and airport closures. CBS News reports at least 20 European flights have faced threats in a week, and quotes an expert who calls the pattern unusual and suggestive of "a very deliberate act." The Financial Times reports experts describe the disruptions as a co-ordinated campaign. No group has been named in the digest reporting.

facts.text: An Aer Lingus flight from Dublin to Rome was diverted to a French military air base at Evreux, Normandy, after a bomb threat, and landed safely.
The French prime minister's office said all 151 passengers and six crew on that flight were safe.
Several other European flights diverted or landed with a military escort after bomb or security threats.
The Guardian reports a WizzAir service from Milan Malpensa to Warsaw was among those affected, citing Italian agency Ansa.
CBS News reports experts call the number of hoaxes in a short period unusual.

stories.headline: ANC support falls sharply in South Africa's municipal elections, early results show
stories.summary: South Africans voted in municipal elections on Wednesday, with nearly 30 million eligible, and early results on Thursday suggest a large drop in support for the governing African National Congress compared with 2021. Final results are still to come. Failing services, infrastructure and corruption were key issues.
stories.why_it_matters: Municipalities run water, electricity and refuse services, so the outcome affects daily life for residents. The results also signal how stable the national coalition politics around the ANC may be.
stories.background: The ANC has led South Africa since the end of apartheid in 1994 but has lost support in recent elections and now governs nationally in coalition. Municipal councils are responsible for local services, which have deteriorated in many cities. Opposition parties contested control of municipalities across the country in this vote.

facts.text: Nearly 30 million people were eligible to vote on Wednesday, November 4.
About 12 million had voted by 5pm on Wednesday, with Gauteng recording the highest turnout, according to a report on AllAfrica.
Reuters reports ANC support fell sharply in early results.
The Financial Times reports early results suggest a huge drop compared with 2021; Bloomberg says modeling based on early results shows the party losing ground.
Corruption, failing infrastructure and deteriorating essential services were among the key issues.

stories.headline: French unions stage nationwide strikes and marches over living costs
stories.summary: Trade unions in France called strikes and marches for Thursday over wages and the cost of living, extending more than a month of unrest. Hundreds of thousands of protesters are expected, and DW reports about 70,000 police and security officers were deployed. Parliamentary talks on next year's budget remain deadlocked, Bloomberg reports.
stories.why_it_matters: Strikes in rail, air traffic, hospitals, schools and postal services can disrupt travel and public services. The unrest is a test for President Emmanuel Macron five months before a presidential election.
stories.background: France has seen weeks of protests over rising living costs, including marches in mid-October in which, per the Japan Times, more than half a million people took part, with violence and looting in some places. Unions are now joining together, with five unions in the national day of action per the BBC. The government has not secured agreement on the 2027 budget in parliament.

facts.text: Unions representing education, rail, public hospitals and postal services called the strike; about 70,000 police and security officers were deployed.
The New York Times reports more than 220 demonstrations were expected across the country on Thursday.
Five unions joined the national day of action, according to the BBC.
The protests come five months before a presidential election, and budget talks in parliament are deadlocked.

stories.headline: Israel's president consults parties on who should try to form the next government
stories.summary: President Isaac Herzog began meeting party leaders on Wednesday to decide whether Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu or rival Gadi Eisenkot gets the first chance to form a coalition after an election in which Netanyahu's bloc lost its majority. Israel's election commission confirmed the results and rejected Netanyahu's fraud claims after auditing 9,069 polling stations, and Herzog accepted the certified results.
stories.why_it_matters: Who forms Israel's government shapes its policy on the Iran war and relations with the United States. Until a government is formed, Netanyahu remains in charge of a caretaker administration.
stories.background: Israel held a parliamentary election last week in which Netanyahu's religious-nationalist bloc lost its majority in the Knesset. The president decides which lawmaker gets the first chance to form a coalition, based on party recommendations. Netanyahu has alleged fraud and, separately, foreign spending to sway the vote. A web report says the nominee has 28 days to form a government, with a possible extension.

facts.text: Herzog began meeting party leaders to decide whether Netanyahu or Eisenkot gets the first chance to form a government.

Netanyahu cited "serious suspicions" of foreign spending to influence the election; the largest Arab-Israeli bloc called the accusations unfounded.

stories.headline: Indonesia deploys thousands of troops in Jakarta amid wiretapping scandal
stories.summary: Indonesia's military deployed more than 20,000 troops to Jakarta after generals were arrested in a wiretapping scandal suspected of targeting President Prabowo Subianto. On Thursday thousands of police and military personnel secured a court appearance by former President Joko Widodo.
stories.why_it_matters: A security build-up in the capital and arrests of senior officers raise questions about stability and civilian-military relations in Southeast Asia's largest economy. Only center and left-leaning outlets appear to cover this in the digest.
stories.background: Indonesian authorities are investigating a wiretapping scandal involving senior police officers. Three senior generals have been detained, including Gen. stories.headline: Stocks rise and Treasury yields fall after Democrats win Congress
stories.summary: U.S. stocks rose on Wednesday after Democrats won control of Congress in Tuesday's midterms, with market data showing the Dow up about 3% and the Nasdaq up about 1.4%. Reporting attributes the move to investor expectations of political gridlock and tighter fiscal discipline, which also pushed Treasury yields to multi-week lows and lifted gold. Technology and AI-linked shares lagged, and Reuters reported S&P 500 futures steady on Thursday with the Nasdaq trailing on chip weakness.
stories.why_it_matters: Lower Treasury yields can eventually ease borrowing costs such as mortgage rates, which sit near 7.2%. Gains in the stock market also flow through to retirement accounts, though some analysts warn the rally may be getting ahead of itself.
stories.background: Voters elected a new Congress on Tuesday, and outlets across the spectrum report that Democrats won both chambers while President Trump remains in office. Investors have historically viewed divided government as a brake on big new spending and policy swings. The 10-year Treasury yield had been near 5%, a level that has weighed on stocks and housing. Some right-leaning outlets also flag possible Democratic scrutiny of Wall Street, crypto, prediction markets and AI data centers.

concept.explanation: The Dow Jones Industrial Average adds up the share prices of 30 large companies and divides by a fixed number, so a stock with a high price moves the index more than one with a low price, regardless of the company's size. The S&P 500 instead weights companies by total market value, so the largest firms dominate. That is why the two can move by very different amounts on the same day, as they did this week. It reaches your wallet through retirement funds: many 401(k) index funds track the S&P 500, not the Dow, so the headline Dow number can overstate or understate what your own account did.

quotes.name: S&P 500
quotes.blurb: 500 of the largest US companies. The standard scoreboard for the US stock market.

quotes.name: Nasdaq Composite
quotes.blurb: Heavy on tech companies, so it swings harder than the S&P 500 on tech news.

quotes.name: Dow Jones Industrial Average
quotes.blurb: 30 big, established US companies. The oldest and most quoted index, but narrow.

quotes.name: Fed funds rate
quotes.blurb: The overnight rate the Federal Reserve targets. Every other US interest rate keys off it.

quotes.name: 2-year Treasury yield
quotes.blurb: What the US government pays to borrow for 2 years. Moves with expectations for Fed rate changes.

quotes.name: 10-year Treasury yield
quotes.blurb: The government's 10-year borrowing cost. Mortgage rates and company borrowing costs follow it.

quotes.name: 30-year mortgage rate
quotes.blurb: Freddie Mac's weekly average for a 30-year fixed mortgage.

quotes.name: Inflation (CPI, year over year)
quotes.blurb: How much consumer prices rose over the past year. The Fed aims for about 2%.

quotes.name: Unemployment rate
quotes.blurb: Share of people looking for work who can't find it. From the monthly jobs report.

quotes.name: Crude oil (WTI)
quotes.blurb: US oil price per barrel. Feeds into gas prices and inflation.

quotes.name: Crude oil (Brent)
quotes.blurb: The global oil benchmark. Jumps on Middle East and Russia supply news.

quotes.name: Natural gas (Henry Hub)
quotes.blurb: US natural gas price at the Henry Hub in Louisiana, per million BTU. Drives heating and electricity bills.

quotes.name: US dollar index (broad)
quotes.blurb: The Fed's index of the dollar against the currencies of US trading partners. Up means a stronger dollar.

quotes.name: Euro (USD per EUR)
quotes.blurb: Dollars per euro. Up means the euro strengthened against the dollar.

quotes.name: Japanese yen (JPY per USD)
quotes.blurb: Yen per dollar. Up means a weaker yen.

quotes.name: Chinese yuan (CNY per USD)
quotes.blurb: Yuan per dollar. Beijing manages it closely, so moves are a policy signal.

quotes.name: Bitcoin
quotes.blurb: The largest cryptocurrency. Trades around the clock and swings far more than stocks.
